Market volatility rose following the midterms, putting the AI trade and data center buildout under renewed scrutiny

NVIDIA, Caterpillar, and Nike headline next week's corporate events, offering important clues on AI investment, construction demand, and the consumer

Procter & Gamble's Investor Day may add further consumer color, with easing energy costs and a bit better labor market potentially supporting the 2027 outlook

If you're hyper-focused on markets and geopolitics, it feels like the world has changed in the past week-plus. The U.S. midterm elections brought about a surprising volatility thrust, first with a premature "clearing event" rally on Wednesday, November 4, followed by 2026's broadest-based selloff on Thursday. The plunge was the Nasdaq 100's biggest since March 2020. The bulls were back in town to kick off this week, though, and all 11 S&P 500® sectors posted Monday gains.

AI on Thin Ice?

Macro storylines have no doubt been rewritten. The AI trade and data center buildout are being called into question ahead of the new, much bluer Congress set to take the reins on Capitol Hill in January. It remains to be seen how throttled AI investment will be in 2027 and beyond, but even before voters cast ballots, price action in data center plays was dismal.

Many chip stocks, shares of data center infrastructure names, and power providers were down 40% or more from their respective 52-week highs. Now, all eyes are on late-season reporters, but more importantly, on what company executives have to say about the megatrend's future.

NVIDIA's Busy Calendar Amid Drama at the Top

The elephant in the room is NVIDIA (NVDA) and CEO Jensen Huang. The so-called "Godfather of AI" has laid low following the news of his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. After a 4% decline on Monday, the world's second-most valuable company is 25% off its early-October record high.

NVIDIA's corporate event calendar remains loaded, with speaking engagements slated early next week at Supercomputing SC 2026, starting Sunday; Microsoft Ignite 2026, beginning Tuesday; and the TomorrowX Summit 2026, kicking off on the 17th as well.

The chip designer and cornerstone of the AI buildout then reports fiscal Q3 2027 earnings that afternoon, presumably with Jensen offering commentary thereafter. No shortage of drama there.

CAT, NKE, and PG Offer Mid-Quarter Updates

Stocks soared Monday.
Credit: Michael Nagle / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Stock indexes appear to be headed in opposite directions, with futures tied to the Dow up and those associated with the Nasdaq 100 pointing lower; the government released the October consumer price index reading, with inflation rising from a month earlier; Fed Governor Christopher Waller suggested the central bank would need to tighten monetary policy "sooner, rather than later"; Anthropic issued fresh details about its planned IPO; and investors are eyeing the latest moves in shares of Nvidia and CoreWeave.

Here's what you need to know today.

Stock Indexes Poised for Mixed Open

Stock futures pointed to a mixed open after a Monday bounce, with futures tied to the Nasdaq 100 down about 0.8% and those associated with the Dow up 0.1%; October CPI data appeared to take some wind out of the morning's outlook. S&P 500 futures were down 0.3% . The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury was near 4.9%, up slightly from last night. Oil prices were also falling, with the global benchmark Brent down about 3% to $89.88 a barrel and the U.S. benchmark, West Texas Intermediate, down more than 2% to below $85 a barrel. Precious metal prices were slipping, as was the price of bitcoin, which was holding above $74,000, according to CoinDesk. Read our live coverage of today's markets here.

Inflation Rose in October Despite Moderation in Oil Prices

The consumer price index rose 0.4% in October, according to data released this morning, cooler than September's 0.6%. Core CPI, which excludes food and energy, was 0.3% higher month on month. Both numbers were hotter than economists expected. The government did not release year-over-year numbers, citing data collection issues; economists anticipated the CPI rising 3.9% in October, up from 3.7% over the 12 months ended in September. Oil prices have come down some since September, but fuel and energy costs remain relatively high because of the war and could continue to push up prices. The Fed will consider inflation when deciding whether to raise interest rates next month. More on that next.

Fed's Waller Urges Tightening 'Sooner, Rather Than Later'

Fed Governor Christopher Waller, a voting member of the central bank's rate-setting committee, in a morning speech—before the inflation data—said inflation remained too high and tightening monetary policy was necessary "sooner, rather than later. Wallace was part of the majority who opted to keep interest rates steady when the Federal Open Market Committee met last month, and he expressed support for getting inflation back to its 2% target in the "medium term," indicating that he would back a 50 basis point hike in December if the data supported it. Traders see a quarter-point hike as a near-certainty, according to the CME's FedWatch tool.

Anthropic IPO Moves Forward

Claude maker Anthropic's planned IPO is chugging ahead. The company in a regulatory filing said it planned to sell more than 800 million shares—with shareholders selling another 25 million—and establish an expected range of $70 to $78 apiece. The implied valuation comes in above $1 trillion, which would make it one of the biggest publicly traded U.S. companies upon arrival, but some investors had expected a number as much as twice that earlier this year. The company is pushing forward amid recent volatility in AI stocks, which may lead other companies to postpone their plans. (Here's our primer on Anthropic's business.)

Nvidia, CoreWeave Shares Slip Premarket

Investors were tracking Nvidia (NVDA) and CoreWeave (CRWV) shares this morning. Nvidia looks poised to open modestly lower this morning, potentially extending yesterday's losses driven by the news that it's investigating CEO Jensen Huang for reportedly having an affair with a Chinese spy. Huang may also have to testify before Congress.

CoreWeave (CRWV) is slated to hand in quarterly numbers this evening, weeks after investors ditched its shares over concerns about its financial health. Analysts expect CoreWeave to report $162 million in net income on $1.3 billion in revenue, according to Visible Alpha. Its shares were recently down about 2% premarket.

Key Takeaways

Verizon stock is up 11% in the past month, winning back its October selloff after SpaceX agreed to buy nationwide wireless spectrum.

Verizon added 406,000 postpaid phones in the third quarter, its best third quarter in five years, and raised guidance for the third straight quarter, though revenue missed as equipment sales fell.

Elon Musk says SpaceX can build a carrier network in two or three years, against Verizon CEO Dan Schulman's four to six, and SpaceX's reported cell-site talks could help tower owner Crown Castle.

Verizon trades near its usual valuation and its dividend is well covered by free cash flow, so the stock still looks like a buy. The FCC's ruling on SpaceX's spectrum deal is the next thing to watch.

Verizon (VZ:NYSE) stock is up 10.6% in the past month, while the Nasdaq 100 fell 9.6%.

That's quite a turnaround from Oct. 9, when Verizon fell 8.75%, its worst day since 2002, after SpaceX (SPCX:NASDAQ) agreed to buy a nationwide block of 800 MHz spectrum for its Starlink Mobile service.

Then Bloomberg reported on Oct. 22 that SpaceX is in talks for at least 80,000 US cell sites, including those of Crown Castle (CCI:NYSE). The carriers slid on the news while tower owners rallied, and Crown Castle has climbed more than 10% since Oct. 9.

TIKR tracks 24 analysts on Verizon. How many say "Buy"?

The quarter beat, and the stock fell anyway

Verizon reported its third quarter on Oct. 26. It added 406,000 postpaid phones, its best third quarter in five years, and postpaid phone churn improved to 0.94% from 0.98%. Free cash flow rose 12.1% to $7.8 billion, and Verizon raised its full-year guidance for the third quarter in a row.

But revenue of $34.3 billion missed estimates, and the stock fell 3.5% that day. Equipment revenue dropped 9%, mostly because customers are upgrading less often and Verizon is spending less on phone subsidies. That shrinks revenue but fattens margins: the adjusted EBITDA margin hit a record 40.2%, up from 37.8%.

CEO Dan Schulman said in the release that "we are only one year into a multi-year growth story." Analysts agree, with normalized EPS climbing from $4.71 in fiscal 2025 to $5.31 in fiscal 2027:

US stock futures were mixed on Tuesday as investors awaited October inflation figures, assessed developments in the conflict involving Iran and monitored corporate news affecting the artificial intelligence sector. Oil prices continued to decline, while Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) shares recovered slightly in after-hours trading following a decline in the previous session.

At 03:17 ET (08:17 GMT), S&P 500 futures were up 13 points, or 0.2%, while Nasdaq 100 futures declined 22 points, or 0.1%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures gained 252 points, or 0.5%.

Wall Street Recovers Following Technology Sector Volatility

Major US equity indices advanced during Monday's session, with the S&P 500 recording its largest daily gain since April.

Semiconductor shares contributed to the recovery, with an industry benchmark posting its largest one-day increase since July following declines during the previous week.

According to Deutsche Bank analysts, the S&P 500 had declined approximately 0.25% over the four trading sessions following the US midterm elections.

The analysts attributed part of the subsequent recovery to changes in investor positioning after the earlier market declines.

They noted that equity allocations had become substantially underweight, while positioning in technology stocks had fallen below levels recorded after the announcement of the US administration's Liberation Day trade measures.

Investors were also assessing whether the Democratic Party's gains in the midterm elections could influence the development of artificial intelligence infrastructure, particularly in states hosting major data centre projects.

October US Inflation Figures in Focus

The US Consumer Price Index report for October was scheduled for release later Tuesday, with economists forecasting a 0.3% monthly increase in headline consumer prices.

Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, was expected to rise 0.2% month on month.

An annual inflation comparison was not expected to be published because the federal government shutdown in 2025 prevented the collection of October 2025 consumer price data.

Alternative data provider Truflation identified energy prices as a significant factor affecting inflation, projecting a 20.7% annual increase in energy costs for October.

Its estimates also indicated a 37.7% year-on-year rise in gasoline prices.

Higher fuel costs have contributed to concerns about household affordability, which featured prominently during the recent US midterm election campaign.

The election resulted in Democratic control of both chambers of Congress, potentially affecting the administration's ability to advance elements of its legislative agenda.

Investing.com - Futures linked to the main U.S. stock indices hover around both sides of the flatline, as investors await key inflation figures and assess fragile sentiment around the artificial intelligence trade. Oil falls to roughly $90 a barrel on hopes for a diplomatic resolution to the Iran war, while Nvidia shares tick higher in after-hours trading following a selloff on Monday triggered by a scandal surrounding CEO Jensen Huang.

Our AI stock portfolio is beating the S&P 500 by 118%. Discover the stocks we're buying and the opportunities we're watching next. Exclusive Yahoo! Finance reader offer: Get 60% off InvestingPro. Subscribe today! »

1. Futures mixed

U.S. stock futures pointed to a mixed open on Tuesday. By 03:17 ET (08:17 GMT), the S&P 500 futures contract had risen by 13 points, or 0.2%, while Nasdaq 100 futures had dipped by 22 points, or 0.1%. The Dow futures contract was higher by 252 points, or 0.5%.

The main averages on Wall Street gained in the prior session, as a renewed bout of dip-buying powered the benchmark S&P 500 to its best day since April. Optimism once again brightened around AI following last week's roller-coaster moves in stocks exposed to the nascent technology, with a tracker of the semiconductor industry in particular notching its largest one-day gain since July.

Following a series of selloffs and recoveries, the S&P 500 is now down "only" 0.25% in the four business days after the U.S. midterm elections, analysts at Deutsche Bank noted. Traders have been attempting to gauge whether a major victory for Democrats, especially in gubernatorial races in states that host massive data center projects, will lead to a slowdown in AI development.

"There wasn't an obvious catalyst for the bounceback, but as our equity strategists noted, equity positioning had become sizably underweight after last week's moves, and in tech, positioning was now beneath its lows after Liberation Day," the Deutsche Bank analysts said.

2. CPI ahead

Attention now turns to the release of monthly U.S. inflation figures. Headline consumer prices are tipped to have risen 0.3% month-over-month in October. The annualized rate will not be released because a federal government shutdown last year prevented the collection of the consumer-price index for October 2025.

The so-called "core" gauge, which strips out volatile items like food and fuel, is seen increasing by 0.2% month-over-month.

Energy is still the "principal swing factor" for overall price gains, flagged analysts at Truflation, an alternative data provider. For October, Truflation has projected a 20.7% rise in energy prices versus a year earlier, with gasoline climbing 37.7%.

Higher costs at the gas pump partially fueled discontentment over affordability that helped drive a sharp rebuke of U.S. President Donald Trump's economic policy in midterm elections. American voters widely supported Democratic challengers to Trump's Republican candidates in several statewide races, giving Democrats control over both chambers of Congress in the process. The victory could make it more difficult for Trump to aggressively pursue his policy goals, including the ongoing war with Iran and tariffs on global trading partners.

Crucially, the outcome of the Labor Department's consumer-price index could sway projections for Federal Reserve interest rates. Solid labor market data last Friday may have given Fed officials more headroom to raise rates next month, after policymakers rolled out their first increase in three years in September. In theory, lifting borrowing costs can quell inflation, albeit at the risk of weighing on overall economic activity and the job market.

3. Oil slips to around $90

Also bolstering stocks has been a downward slide in oil prices, which has dragged the benchmark Brent crude futures contract to roughly $90 a barrel. As recently as late October, Brent was exchanging hands at over $115 a barrel, as markets fretted over the prospect of new and intense U.S. attacks on Iran in the wake of the midterms.

However, diplomatic efforts have appeared to gain momentum. Trump has signaled that he would like to find an end to the war with Iran, a conflict now in its ninth month that has been partly responsible for pushing up energy prices and elevating inflation.

The president's comments came after a meeting with the prime minister of Qatar, a frequent mediator between Washington and Tehran. Still, Trump warned that U.S. is "locked and loaded," while describing Iran's military as "effectively over." Citing an official familiar with the matter, Bloomberg News reported that talks between the U.S. and Iran will carry on and there will likely not be a fresh military escalation.

4. Nvidia shares in focus amid Huang scandal

Elsewhere, shares of Nvidia edged higher in extended hours trading after the AI-darling fell by more than 4% following the company's announcement of an independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang.

In a memo to employees, Huang admitted to having a romantic relationship with a businesswoman from a Singapore-based firm who was allegedly a spy for China. The news has rattled Nvidia, who has become a bellwether -- and frequent financial backstop -- of the AI industry under Huang.

Speaking to reporters during a press briefing at the White House, Trump said "I know the FBI is looking into [Huang] and I think that he'll be in good shape."

"I asked him that question. Did you have any idea that she was a spy? He said I had no idea that she was a spy and I really believe him," Trump said.

5. Anthropic's roughly $70 billion IPO plan retracted after circulated to banks - Reuters

Anthropic may begin formally marketing its potential blockbuster initial public offering on Tuesday, giving the Claude-maker the opportunity to pitch itself as a solid investment despite broader ructions in the AI sector.

The company reportedly sent bankers details of the IPO before retracting the pricing information, saying the figures were inaccurate, Reuters reported on Monday, citing emails seen by the news agency.

Anthropic initially circulated a copy of an IPO filing indicating plans to offer about 867 million shares at a price range of $70 to $80 apiece, potentially raising as much as $69.3 billion. But it later sent another email to bankers saying the pricing details were inaccurate and that an updated filing would be provided later, according to the Reuters report.

title: One Bad Day: A levered-QQQ ETF Case Study
detail:
One Bad Day: A levered-QQQ ETF Case Study
Dave Nadig
Mon, November 9, 2026 at 6:03 PM MST 4 min read
QQQ
^NDX
TQQQ
SQQQ
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Best ETFs - Long Term - QQQ

You might have noticed a little sell off last week. On Thursday November 5th, markets sold off hard, and the Nasdaq 100 -- most commonly tracked by the Invesco QQQ™ ETF, QQQ. (Yes, the legal name of the fund includes it's own ticker) closed down over 6%.

One of the things that happens on a big move is that any geared funds -- anything from 1.2X to 3X to their inverse versions -- has to also make some big buys or sells. So when something as trader-friendly as the Qs is play, the street learns the story pretty fast. By 3:30, here's where the smart money on #FinTwit was headed:

So who's right here? Morgan Stanley saying "$50bn in selling to come!" or Jay Dilks saying "Buying opportunity!"

Let's do the numbers. Let's look very narrowly just at TQQQ (the 3x ETF from ProShares) and it's sister, the short version, SQQQ.

Both funds had to be substantial sellers into the close. It tends to break peoples brains that both the long and the short ETF have the same trade, but here's the simplest chart I can make with Claude to illustrate it:

TQQQ started Thursday with $33.54 billion in net assets (the biggest fund in our leveraged/inverse universe.) Since it's daily mandate is 3X, that means the fund had to have $100.61 billion of notional exposure (through swaps). Then the Nasdaq-100 fell 6.3556%.

Applying that move to starting exposure leaves $94.21 billion left over in the swap. But TQQQ's actual NAV fell 19.0969%, shrinking the actual AUM of the fund from $33.5 billion to just $27.13 billion. This is a real problem for the portfolio manager, because they know the next morning, when the circus starts all over, they only want to be 300% exposed. Now just a $27.13 billion fund, they only need $81.39 billion in exposure tomorrow.

That's a $12.82 billion lightening of exposure, sometime between roughly 3:30 and the close.

SQQQ has the same problem in reverse. It started with $1.83B in assets, and thus negative-$5.4 billion in exposure. The fund crushed it, rising over 19% on the day (as you'd hope!), bringing new AUM to $2.18 billion, and thus needing negative-$6.53 billion in exposure. The implied net sell for SQQQ is another $1.4 billion.

So, two funds, going different directions, both making the sell off worse, at the margin.

Buying the Dip?

Back to the original tweet from Jay here... does that mean you should buy the dip?

In general I'm skeptical. Here's the two big indexes going into Thursday's close:

I can't perfectly tie the last-minute selloff to the tape getting wind of the levered complex trade. Everyone knows about it, it's easy to calculate, so there's never a surprise. It's just a question of how baked into the end of day trading prices the known-accelerant is at any given point in time. Personally, I think that's impossible to call: the Qs could have rallied into the close because Mercury entered retrograde, who knows.

Wall Street gained $1tn (£740bn) on Monday after shrugging off fears of an AI bubble and a national security scandal at Nvidia.

Stock markets enjoyed their best day for seven months, propelled by hopes of falling oil prices after Donald Trump claimed fresh Iran strikes were "highly unlikely".

The relief rally marks a sharp reversal from last week, when fears of a crackdown on AI data centres sent tech shares falling by their most in six years.

The S&P 500 rose 2.4pc, the Nasdaq 100 gained 3.4pc and the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed up 2.2pc.

The boost came as Andrew Bailey warned that bets on AI could take years to pay off, risking a further sell-off by disappointed investors.

Mr Bailey, the Governor of the Bank of England, said the financial benefits of the new technology will "take longer to be realised than predicted".

Speaking in Switzerland, he warned of the risk of an AI bubble, citing Thomas Edison, who took years to commercialise electricity after inventing the light bulb.

"The returns may be good, and they may match expectations, but they take longer to be realised than predicted.

"This has been the case historically with big general purpose technology innovation – take Edison and electricity, for instance. There are good reasons to believe that the world moves faster now, but still the timing may not live up to market expectations."

Fears had grown last week that the AI boom was about to unravel after the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 fell by the most since 2020.

This was triggered by the Democrats' midterm election victory, which had prompted fears of a slowdown in the data centre construction central to the growth of AI.

However, investors on Wall Street partially shrugged of their concerns on Monday, sending shares up across the board.

The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index, a grouping of the world's largest chip developers, rallied as much as 7pc.

Fresh revelations that Jensen Huang, the Nvidia's founder and chief, had admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy also failed to stem the Nasdaq rally despite Nvidia shares falling as much as 8pc.

Chris Larkin, from Morgan Stanley, said: "There's good reason to believe the stock market's long-term rally is intact."

David Solomon, the chief executive at Goldman Sachs, also attempted to boost confidence by predicting even more investment investment in data centres and AI infrastructure.

"The market is open and transactions are happening," he said.

The direction of oil prices offered further confidence to investors on inflation, after Mr Trump played down the likelihood of further strikes on Iran.

US stock indices settled sharply higher on Monday as dip buyers stepped in to buy recently beaten-down chipmakers and AI-infrastructure stocks. The Magnificent Seven technology stocks also rallied on Monday, supporting gains in the broader market. In addition, market sentiment improved after WTI crude oil sank more than -4% as diplomatic efforts to end the war in Iran continue.

Hawkish Fed comments on Monday were bearish for stocks and bonds. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said US employment and growth are pretty stable, but inflation is starting to kick up in services, and we've got to come to terms with inflation failure. Also, Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin said robust demand and stubbornly high inflation mean interest rates will need to go higher, though any rate hikes will need to be done at a careful pace.

Dec WTI crude oil prices (CLZ26) tumbled more than -4% on Monday to a 2.25-month low on optimism that diplomatic progress is gaining momentum to end the US-Iran war, which could lead to a full resumption of energy supplies from the Middle East. President Trump said it's "highly unlikely" he'll order more strikes against Iran if peace talks show progress. Axios reported that President Trump met the prime minister of Qatar on Monday to focus on negotiations with Iran. Crude oil losses accelerated Monday after news outlet Israel Hayom reported that Iran dropped its demand to control the Strait of Hormuz and collect transit fees from vessels passing through the waterway.
